findings.exact_estimate: Descriptive geospatial/cluster statistics (no p-values reported in main text): 60% of irrigation districts with pre-1914 senior water rights have surface water allocations equal to twice crop water demand (up to 3x on eastern side), whereas 86% of all San Joaquin Valley irrigation districts rely on groundwater for irrigation and 12% rely exclusively on groundwater. In cluster analysis, Senior, Secure Nut Growers (SSN, n = 7 older districts) have 31 to 50 ML/Ha surface water allocations and 30% groundwater reliance (vs. 81% in FCC [n = 27], 93% in SCG [n = 14], 100% in CCB, and heavy reliance in GDV), yet DACs inside SSN still average an 86% CalEnviroScreen vulnerability percentile (PDF Pages 1, 11, 14-16).
findings.exposure_and_reference: Older irrigation districts formed in the Era of Local Organization (1887-1913) with senior pre-1914 surface water rights vs. younger irrigation districts formed post-1914 (Hydraulic Era 1914-1968, Era of Conflict 1969-2000, Era of Reconciliation 2001-2020) with junior or no surface water rights.
findings.finding_label: Agricultural irrigation supply outcome: Surface water allocations and agricultural groundwater dependence across water-rights eras/clusters
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Agricultural irrigation district surface water allocation/delivery (ML/Ha; HIGHER = greater agricultural irrigation water supply) and agricultural groundwater dependence (%; LOWER = greater agricultural surface-water security). Explicitly excludes domestic and municipal drinking-water agencies.

headline_result_summary: In an observational geospatial and cross-sectional comparison of 153 Disadvantaged Communities (DACs) on California's San Joaquin Valley floor, communities located within agricultural irrigation district jurisdictions (ID-DACs, n = 97) do not have better household drinking-water or groundwater conditions than groundwater-dependent communities outside irrigation district boundaries (GDCs, n = 56): unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon tests on CalEnviroScreen 4.0 percentiles find null differences for Poor Drinking Water Exposure (mean 83% in ID-DACs vs. 79% in GDCs, p = 0.1363) and Threats to Groundwater (mean 56% vs. 55%, p = 0.829), while ID-DACs experience significantly worse non-water Pollution Exposure (81% vs. 74%, p = 0.005413) and Pesticide Exposure (83% vs. 77%, p = 0.00965). Separately, descriptive water-budget and cluster analyses of agricultural irrigation districts (explicitly excluding domestic and municipal water agencies) show that older districts with pre-1914 senior water rights hold far larger agricultural surface-water allocations (60% hold twice their crop water demand) and lower agricultural groundwater reliance than post-1914 junior districts, but this agricultural water wealth does not translate into better drinking-water access or lower vulnerability for resident DACs.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: Four major coding traps exist in this paper: (1) Outcome polarity inversion in Table 1: 'Poor Drinking Water Exposure (%)' and 'Threats to Groundwater (%)' are CalEnviroScreen hazard/exposure percentiles where HIGHER numbers mean WORSE water quality/greater contamination risk, NOT better access; ID-DACs have numerically slightly higher (worse) poor drinking water exposure than GDCs (83% vs. 79%), though statistically non-significant. (2) Over-interpreting non-significant differences: both water-related community indicators in Table 1 are null at alpha = 0.05 (p = 0.1363 and p = 0.829). (3) Conflating agricultural irrigation surface-water allocations with household water access: Section 2.2 explicitly states that the district-level analysis excludes domestic and municipal water agencies and studies only agricultural irrigation supply; the paper's central 'paradox of production' finding is precisely that senior pre-1914 agricultural surface-water rights increase farm irrigation supply without improving community drinking water or vulnerability (DACs in the 'Senior, Secure Nut Growers' cluster still average an 86% CalEnviroScreen vulnerability percentile). (4) Mistaking statistically significant non-water rows in Table 1 (Pollution Exposure p = 0.005413, Pesticide Exposure p = 0.00965, PM2.5 Exposure p = 0.03291, or Population p = 0.003456) for household water-service outcomes.
study_design: Cross-sectional geospatial, water-budget, cluster, and two-group observational comparison (unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for DAC indicators; descriptive historical-era and k-cluster analyses for irrigation districts).
unit_and_sample_size: Community-level comparison: N = 153 Disadvantaged Communities (DAC census places matched to CalEnviroScreen 4.0 census-tract indicators) on the San Joaquin Valley floor, comprising n = 97 DACs inside irrigation district boundaries (ID-DACs) and n = 56 DACs outside irrigation district boundaries in groundwater-dependent communities (GDCs). District-level agricultural water-budget/cluster analysis: irrigation districts across the 8 San Joaquin Valley counties (excluding water conservation, domestic, and municipal water agencies; exact total district count not summed in main text, partial cluster counts reported: SCG = 14, FCC = 27, SSN = 7, plus GDV and CCB).
